scenes.tts: A message arrives at the tip of an axon. How does it get home? One answer is a courier. A courier carries one parcel the whole way. The other is a bucket brigade. Each stretch of the axon hands the message to the next, and nothing physical makes the whole journey.
scenes.visual: Two axon lanes: a parcel rides the whole length in the courier lane; a message hops stretch to stretch in the brigade lane.
scenes.narration: A message arrives at the tip of an axon. How does it get home? One answer is a courier. A courier carries one parcel the whole way. The other is a bucket brigade. Each stretch of the axon hands the message to the next, and nothing physical makes the whole journey.

scenes.tts: The popular test is to block dynein, the motor. In 2004, Heerssen, Pazyra and Segal found that dynein motors transport activated T R K receptors. They found that this transport is needed for the survival of neurons that depend on their target. That is real evidence for a courier.
scenes.caption: The popular test is to block dynein, the motor. In 2004, Heerssen, Pazyra and Segal found that dynein motors transport activated Trk receptors. They found that this transport is needed for the survival of neurons that depend on their target. That is real evidence for a courier.
scenes.visual: Courier lane: dynein motor carries the parcel; block it and it stalls; evidence tag appears.
scenes.narration: The popular test is to block dynein, the motor. In 2004, Heerssen, Pazyra and Segal found that dynein motors transport activated Trk receptors. They found that this transport is needed for the survival of neurons that depend on their target. That is real evidence for a courier.

scenes.tts: A brigade would fail the same test, though. Suppose each stretch of the axon needs dynein-driven transport for its own local step. Then blocking dynein stops the brigade as completely as it stops the courier. So the block cannot tell them apart.
scenes.visual: Brigade lane: a dynein mark in each stretch; the block stops both lanes the same way.

scenes.tts: The relay is a published alternative. In 2002, MacInnis and Campenot reported that retrograde signals can support neuron survival without retrograde transport of N G F itself. In 2003, Ye, Kuruvilla, Zweifel and Ginty titled their paper: Evidence in support of signaling endosome-based retrograde survival of sympathetic neurons. The title claims support. It does not claim proof. Settled: N G F at the terminal is enough, a signal from the terminal reaches the nucleus, and dynein carries activated receptors that survival depends on. Not settled: whether the carried receptor is the only route.
